analysis.answer: Compared to current law, which allows parents to fund an education savings account with 90 percent of state per-pupil funding for private educational uses, the measure repeals the program and reverts unspent funds to the state school fund.

The state saves the 90 percent per-pupil funding that would have been diverted to private accounts. Families currently using the program face the opportunity cost of losing subsidized private education.

Public school systems benefit by retaining full per-pupil funding and acquiring any remaining account balances. Parents who would have used the accounts bear the cost of paying for alternative education out of pocket.

Parents may shift their children back into the public school system, potentially increasing public school enrollment. Alternatively, they may keep their children in private alternatives and bear the full tuition cost.
The measure addresses the diversion of state education funds to private accounts. The mechanism of outright repeal ends the program, ensuring those funds remain in the public school system.
Public school districts gain resources and retain students who might otherwise have transferred to alternative education providers.

The effect of education savings accounts on student achievement and public school finances is disputed. Some researchers find that such programs improve outcomes through competition, while others argue they primarily subsidize families already inclined toward private education and negatively impact public school budgets.
Ending the program will eliminate its ongoing administrative costs, though there may be short-term efforts required to close accounts and transfer remaining balances.
This is a statutory change that can be reversed by future legislation.

flags.note: The repeal and reversion of funds are delayed until July 2028.
